items.name: Resonance curve best fit and peak
items.how: Given V (mV) and f (kHz) data for an electrical resonance circuit plotted as a graph: (i) draw a line of best fit, (ii) estimate the maximum V, (iii) state the resonant frequency.
items.ms: (i) smooth curve through/close to the points, peak clearly at or below 25 kHz (2); (ii) maximum V between 27 and 35 mV, consistent with their peak, unit required (1); (iii) peak frequency read correctly with unit (1).

items.name: Improve accuracy of resonant frequency
items.how: Suggest one way the experiment could be improved to give a more accurate resonant frequency.
items.ms: Take more readings of V and f near the peak (e.g. between 20 and 25 kHz) at smaller frequency increments (1).

items.name: Capacitor discharge circuit diagram
items.how: Draw a circuit diagram to investigate current against time as two identical series capacitors discharge through a resistor and ammeter.
items.ms: Capacitors in series with a d.c. supply (1); discharge circuit through resistor and ammeter (1); a method of switching between charging and discharging (1).

items.name: Safety precaution with charged capacitors
items.how: State one safety precaution the student should take.
items.ms: Ensure the working p.d. of the capacitors is not exceeded, or connect them with the correct polarity, or ensure they are fully discharged after the experiment (1).

items.name: Determine total capacitance using stopwatch
items.how: Describe how the student, using a stopwatch and the discharge circuit, should determine an accurate value for the total capacitance.
items.ms: Record current with the ammeter; start stopwatch as discharge starts; keep ammeter and stopwatch close or use lap timer; record corresponding I and t; at least 5 sets of readings; plot ln I against t, gradient = -1/RC. Alternative end: time for current to halve or fall to 37%, using t half = RC ln 2 or time constant = RC.

deps.name: Capacitor discharge circuit diagram

items.name: Data logger advantage in discharge experiment
items.how: Suggest why using a data logger instead of a stopwatch and ammeter would improve the discharge investigation.
items.ms: Current and time readings are taken simultaneously (1); many readings can be taken in a short time / higher sample rate (1).

deps.name: Determine total capacitance using stopwatch

items.name: Calipers technique, mean and uncertainty
items.how: (i) Explain one technique to reduce the uncertainty in measuring a ring's hole diameter with digital calipers. (ii) Determine the mean of four readings (8.53, 8.56, 8.55, 8.53 mm) and its uncertainty.
items.ms: (i) 2 marks: repeat at different orientations and take a mean to reduce random error; or check and correct zero error to reduce systematic error. (ii) 3 marks: mean d = 8.54 mm (1); half-range calculation (1); uncertainty 0.02 mm, consistent decimal places (1).

items.name: Uncertainty in d squared and ring area
items.how: (i) Show the uncertainty in d^2 is about 1 mm^2 for d = 10.70 +/- 0.06 mm. (ii) Show the percentage uncertainty in A = (pi/4)(s^2 - d^2) is about 0.4%, given s^2 = 881 +/- 2 mm^2.
items.ms: (i) 3 marks: %U in d = 0.56% (1); double it for d^2 (1); U = 1.3 mm^2 (1); or max/min d^2 half-range. (ii) 4 marks: A = 602 mm^2; add uncertainties in s^2 and d^2 (with ecf); multiply by pi/4; %U = 0.43%. Or use maximum/minimum A.

items.name: Ring density and stainless steel check
items.how: (i) Determine the mean density in g cm^-3 of the ring metal from a 10-ring stack (mass 63.0 +/- 0.5 g, thickness 14.03 +/- 0.04 mm, A = 602 mm^2 +/- 0.4%). (ii) Deduce whether it could be stainless steel (7.48 to 7.95 g cm^-3).
items.ms: (i) 2 marks: rho = m / (x A) = 7.46 g cm^-3 (3 s.f.). (ii) 3 marks: %U in rho = 1.5% (adding %U in m, x and A); upper limit 7.57 g cm^-3 (or %difference 0.3% < %U); 7.57 > 7.48 so it could be stainless steel.

deps.name: Uncertainty in d squared and ring area

items.name: Why log-log graph gives straight line + Plot log-log graph; find n and k
items.how: From a table of atomic number Z and frequency f (in units of 10^15 Hz) for six elements: (i) plot log Z against log f using the processed-data space, (ii) determine n, (iii) determine k using the graph.
items.ms: (i) 6 marks: log Z and log f values correct to 2 d.p., axes labelled with units (log (f / 10^15 Hz)), appropriate scales, accurate plotting, best-fit line. (ii) 3 marks: large gradient triangle, n in range 0.45 to 0.50, 2 or 3 s.f. no unit. (iii) 3 marks: y-intercept (log k about 0.86), k in range 6.9 to 7.3, 2 or 3 s.f.

items.name: Why log-log graph gives straight line + Plot log-log graph; find n and k + Does graph support Moseley relationship
items.how: Explain whether the graph supports Moseley's suggestion that Z is proportional to f^0.5.
items.ms: Identify that the gradient (n) would be 0.5 for Z proportional to f^0.5 (1); conclusion from comparing the calculated n (about 0.48) with 0.5, so the graph supports the suggestion (1). Alternative: substitute their k and n into Z = k f^n.

items.name: Accurate single height measurement and uncertainty
items.how: (i) Describe a method to measure the height h of a bulb above a light sensor accurately with a metre rule. (ii) Explain why an uncertainty of 1 mm is appropriate for h = 368 mm.
items.ms: (i) 3 marks: clamp the rule vertical (check with set square/plumb line) close to the sensor; zero at the sensor surface or subtract two readings; view the scale perpendicularly. (ii) 3 marks: resolution is 1 mm; uncertainty of one reading is half the resolution (0.5 mm); two judgements so 0.5 + 0.5 = 1 mm.

items.name: Signal generator frequency and resonance plan
items.how: (a) Show that a signal generator trace on an oscilloscope (0.5 ms per division) has frequency about 700 Hz. (b) Devise a plan, including a graph, to find X in f^2 = X / C for a coil, capacitor and resistor circuit with an ammeter at maximum current.
items.ms: (a) 4 marks: count divisions for at least two waves, multiply by 0.5 ms, T from the number of waves, f = 1/T in range 667 to 690 Hz (e.g. 682 Hz). (b) 6 marks: vary f until the ammeter reading is a maximum; find T from the oscilloscope and f = 1/T; record f for different C (at least 5 sets); plot f^2 against 1/C and use the gradient for X (or log f against log C, intercept).

items.name: Radioactive decay count rate investigation
items.how: Full question on a G-M tube and beta source: (a) two safety precautions, (b) obtaining the source count rate, (c)(i) using ln C against t to get lambda, (ii) plot ln C against t with processed-data table, (iii) determine lambda from the graph, (iv) effect of a shorter half-life on the graph.
items.ms: (a) tongs, minimum time, keep away from the source, lid on bottle (any 2). (b) record background count rate and subtract from all readings (2). (c)(i) ln C = ln C0 - lambda t, gradient -lambda (2). (ii) ln C values to 3 d.p. (4.771, 4.489, 4.190, 3.892, 3.664), labelled axes, scales, plotting, best-fit line (5). (iii) large triangle, lambda about 9.35 x 10^-3 s^-1, range 0.0092 to 0.0098, positive, unit s^-1 (3). (iv) shorter half-life gives larger lambda so a steeper graph (3).

items.name: Micrometer uncertainty and reducing error
items.how: (i) Determine the percentage uncertainty in a micrometer reading of the rod diameter (2.34 mm). (ii) Explain one technique, other than correcting zero error, to reduce the error in d.
items.ms: (i) half the resolution = 0.005 mm (1); %U = 0.2% (0.21%) (1). (ii) repeat at different orientations and calculate a mean (1) to reduce the effect of random error (1, dependent).

items.name: Modulus G calculation and uncertainty
items.how: Using G = 32 m g l x^2 / (pi y d^4) with four d readings, m = 100 g, l, x and y with uncertainties: (i) show G is about 8 x 10^10 Pa, (ii) show the percentage uncertainty in G is about 9%, (iii) deduce whether the rod could be carbon steel (G = 7.70 x 10^10 Pa).
items.ms: (i) 3 marks: mean d = 2.35 mm, substitute into the formula, G = 7.9 x 10^10 Pa. (ii) 4 marks: half-range for d (0.02 mm); %U in l, x, y and d; total %U = %l + 2 %x + %y + 4 %d = 9.4% (or max/min G half-range). (iii) 2 marks: lower limit 7.13 x 10^10 Pa < 7.70 x 10^10 Pa so it could be carbon steel (or %difference 2.2% < 9%).

items.name: Health and safety when heating water
items.how: Identify one health and safety issue with an immersion heater heating water around a fixed-volume flask, and how to deal with it.
items.ms: A hazard (hot heater, beaker, flask or water causing burns or spills, or leads toppling the beaker) (1) with the matching control (switch off before removing, tongs or insulated gloves, clamp the heater) (1).

items.name: Accurate method for temperature of trapped air
items.how: Describe an accurate method to determine a single value of the temperature of the fixed volume of air in the flask heated by a water bath.
items.ms: Use a thermometer in the water (1); place it close to the flask or opposite the heater (1); stir to ensure thermal equilibrium, or read the scale perpendicularly (1).

items.name: Mean temperature, uncertainty, number of molecules
items.how: (i) Determine the mean of four theta readings (42.5, 41.0, 42.0, 43.5 deg C); (ii) determine the percentage uncertainty in the mean; the mark scheme also has (iii), absent from the extracted stem, for the number of air molecules using pV = NkT with the flask volume (4 marks).
items.ms: (i) Mean 42.3 deg C, 1 d.p. (1). (ii) Half range 1.25 deg C (1); about 3% e.c.f. (1). (iii) Convert to kelvin (1), V = 4/3 pi r^3 (1), use pV = NkT (1), N = 4.5 x 10^22 (1).

items.name: Circuit to vary bulb power input
items.how: Complete the circuit diagram for varying the power input to a 12 V filament bulb.
items.ms: Power supply with a means of varying current (1); voltmeter in parallel across the bulb and ammeter in series (1).

items.name: Devise test of P proportional to X^4
items.how: Devise a method, including a suitable graph, to test the prediction P = kX^4 relating bulb power P to light received X (lux) at a light sensor.
items.ms: Keep sensor-to-bulb distance and alignment constant (1); remove background light (1); record I and V (1); calculate P = IV (1); at least 5 values of X for different P (1); plot P against X^4 and check for a straight line, or log P against log X and check straight line / gradient 4 (1).

items.name: Why not record amplitude to nearest mm
items.how: Give two reasons why the amplitude of a damped pendulum should not be recorded to the nearest mm against a half-metre rule.
items.ms: Hard to judge the moment of maximum displacement because the pendulum moves quickly and changes direction (1); hard to keep the line of sight perpendicular to the scale, or the cone is not close to the rule (1).

items.name: ln A against n graph for damped pendulum
items.how: (i) Explain how a graph of ln A against n gives lambda for A = A0 e^(-lambda n); the extracted stem shows only (i), but the mark scheme also covers (ii) plotting ln A against n (5), (iii) lambda from the gradient (3), (iv) A0 from the intercept (3) and (v) why extrapolating to find A0 may be unreliable (2).
items.ms: (i) ln A = ln A0 - lambda n compared with y = c + mx, gradient -lambda (2). (ii) ln A to 3 d.p. (2 d.p. accepted), labelled axes, scales, accurate plotting, best-fit line. (iii) Large triangle, lambda between 0.0335 and 0.0384, positive, no unit. (iv) Intercept 2.295, A0 = e^intercept about 9.9 cm. (v) Scatter, systematic error, or large initial angle undermines the extrapolated line.

items.name: Why height difference uncertainty is 1 mm
items.how: Explain why it was appropriate to record the uncertainty in the difference in height (21 mm) as 1 mm when each height was measured with a metre rule.
items.ms: Resolution of the rule is 1 mm (1); uncertainty in a single measurement is half the resolution, 0.5 mm (1); as the heights are subtracted the uncertainties add to 1 mm (1, dependent on MP2).

items.name: Marker position and percentage uncertainty in time
items.how: Discuss how moving marker 2 to the lower end of the ramp could affect the percentage uncertainty in the time t for a sphere to travel between the markers.
items.ms: Distance s increases so t increases (1); absolute uncertainty in t stays the same (1); so percentage uncertainty in t decreases (1, dependent on MP1 or MP2).

items.name: Calculate g, its percentage uncertainty, accuracy
items.how: (i) Determine g from t^2 = 14s^2/(5g delta-h) with s = 90.0 cm, delta-h = 21 mm, t = 3.36 s; (ii) show the percentage uncertainty in g is about 7%; the mark scheme also has (iii), absent from the extracted stem, deciding whether the value is accurate against 9.81 m s^-2 (2 marks).
items.ms: (i) Rearrange to g = 14s^2/(5t^2 delta-h) (1); g = 9.6 m s^-2 (9.57), 2 or 3 s.f. (1). (ii) %U: 2 x %U in s + %U in delta-h + 2 x %U in t = 0.22 + 4.76 + 1.78 = 6.8% (3), or max/min g half-range method. (iii) Upper limit 10.3 exceeds 9.81, or %D 2.1% < %U, so accurate (2).

items.name: Accurate horizontal range of projectile in sand
items.how: Describe a method to determine an accurate value for the horizontal distance x from the end of a track to where a sphere lands in sand, using a metre rule on the ground.
items.ms: Find the point vertically below the end of the track with a plumb line or large spirit level (1); measure to the centre of the imprint of the sphere (1); view the scale perpendicularly or use a set square to read the rule (1).

items.name: Variation in landing positions; precision comparison
items.how: (i) Explain why the final positions of five identical spheres varied between repeats (Student A and Student B plan views given); the mark scheme also has (ii), absent from the extracted stem, judging a statement comparing the two students' sets of x values (4 marks).
items.ms: (i) Each sphere left the track with a different velocity (1), as the release height differed, release forces differed, path not parallel to the track, or friction differed (1). (ii) Student A has the smaller range of x (1), so more precise (1); there is no true value of x to judge accuracy (1); so the statement is invalid or only partially valid (1).

items.name: Devise method to find K from T and L
items.how: Devise a method, including a suitable graph, to determine K for rotational oscillations of a mass on a wire, where T = 2 pi sqrt(R^2 L / 5K).
items.ms: Measure the mass diameter with calipers or micrometer (1); repeat at different orientations, check zero error or start timing after several oscillations (1); timing marker at the equilibrium position (1); time multiple oscillations and divide (1); at least 5 values of T for different L (1); plot T^2 against L with gradient 4 pi^2 R^2 / 5K (1).

items.name: Cup velocity from generator oscilloscope trace
items.how: (i) Determine the linear velocity of the anemometer cups from an oscilloscope trace (200 ms per division, radius 18 cm); the mark scheme also has (ii), absent from the extracted stem, for how the trace changes (2 marks).
items.ms: (i) Divisions for at least 2 cycles (1); multiply by 200 ms per division to get T = 0.752 s (1); use T = 2 pi/omega and v = r omega (1); v about 1.50 m s^-1, range 1.49 to 1.57 (1). (ii) Peaks closer together or more peaks (1); amplitude increases (1).

items.name: Log-log graph of wind speed against Beaufort number
items.how: (i) Explain how a graph of log v against log B gives p and z for v = pB^z; the extracted stem shows only (i), but the mark scheme also covers (ii) plotting log v against log B (6), (iii) finding z (3), (iv) finding p (3) and (v) predicting v at B = 10 (2).
items.ms: (i) log v = log p + z log B compared with y = c + mx, gradient z and intercept log p (2). (ii) Log values to 3 d.p. (2 d.p. accepted), labelled axes, scales, accurate plotting, best-fit line (6). (iii) Large triangle, z about 1.47, positive, no unit (3). (iv) Intercept about -0.058, p = 10^intercept about 0.875 (3). (v) v = pB^z at B = 10 about 25.8 m s^-1 or read from graph at log B = 1 (2).

items.name: Technique to measure cone height accurately
items.how: Describe a technique to determine an accurate value for the height h of a metal cone using a metre rule.
items.ms: EITHER set square or plumb line to keep the rule vertical (1), clamp the rule (1), rest a set square on the tip of the cone or read horizontally with it (1); OR measure the base diameter (1) and slope length (1) and use Pythagoras for h (1).

items.name: Cone density, uncertainty and material check
items.how: (i) Show that the density of the cone (V = pi d^2 h/12, m = 60.5 g, mean d from four readings, h = 2.93 cm) is about 8.9 g cm^-3; the extracted stem shows only (i), but the mark scheme also has (ii) percentage uncertainty in density (4) and (iii) deciding whether the cone is brass of density 8.53 g cm^-3 (2).
items.ms: (i) Mean d = 29.85 mm (1); V = pi d^2 h/12 = 6.835 cm^3 (1); rho = m/V (1); rho = 8.85 g cm^-3 to at least 3 s.f. (1). (ii) %U in d (half range), 2 x %U in d, add %U in h and m: 0.96%, or max/min method. (iii) Lower limit about 8.77 above 8.53, or %D 3.9% greater than 0.96%, so not brass (2).

items.name: Capacitor safety and charge-sharing circuit
items.how: (i) Describe two safety precautions for electrolytic capacitors; the mark scheme also has (ii), absent from the extracted stem, completing a circuit in which the 680 uF capacitor is connected to a second capacitor X with a voltmeter (2 marks).
items.ms: (i) Any two: do not exceed the working p.d.; correct polarity; discharge fully before handling (1 each). (ii) Voltmeter across the 680 uF capacitor only (1); capacitor X connected in parallel with it (1).

items.name: Criticise graph of V2 against V1
items.how: Criticise a student's plotted graph of V2 against V1 for two capacitors sharing charge (V1 up to 7 V, V2 up to about 1.2 V).
items.ms: Not enough data points (1); range of data too small, or the scales too small (1); spread of data about the best-fit line unreasonable, or the best-fit line may not be linear (1). Ignore comments on s.f., repeats, intervals or the origin.

items.name: Method to estimate absolute zero from gas pressure
items.how: Devise a method, including additional apparatus and a suitable graph, to estimate absolute zero using a fixed volume of air in a flask with pressure gauge and thermometer between 0 and 100 deg C.
items.ms: Place the flask in ice (1); heat with a hot plate, water bath or similar (1); heat gradually, stir, or read the thermometer perpendicularly (1); record temperature and pressure (1); at least 5 different temperatures or intervals of 20 deg C or less (1); plot pressure against temperature and extrapolate to zero pressure, or use gradient and intercept (1).

items.name: Data logger improving pressure and temperature accuracy
items.how: Explain how a data logger with a temperature probe and pressure sensor could improve the accuracy of the measurements.
items.ms: Simultaneous recording of pressure and temperature (1); probe has better resolution, smaller uncertainty or less parallax than a thermometer (1); so readings are closer to the true values (1, dependent on MP1 or MP2).

items.name: Micrometer suitability for slide thickness
items.how: Explain, with a calculation, why a micrometer screw gauge was appropriate to measure a glass slide thickness of 1.21 mm.
items.ms: Micrometer resolution 0.01 mm or uncertainty 0.005 mm (1); so percentage uncertainty = 0.005/1.21 x 100 = 0.4%, which is small (1).

items.name: Control variable in light absorption experiment
items.how: Explain one variable the student should control when measuring the solar cell p.d. for different thicknesses of glass.
items.ms: EITHER the distance between bulb and slides/solar cell (1) because intensity follows an inverse square law (1); OR the background light level (1) since variation changes the voltmeter reading (1). 'Keep the intensity constant' alone not accepted.

items.name: ln V against w graph and number of slides
items.how: (i) Explain how a graph of ln V against w gives B for V = Ae^(-Bw); the extracted stem is cut off after (ii), but the mark scheme also covers (ii) plotting ln V against w (5), (iii) finding the gradient (3) and (iv) number of slides needed to reduce V to 75% of A (4).
items.ms: (i) ln V = ln A - Bw compared with y = c + mx, gradient -B (2). (ii) ln V to 3 d.p. (2 d.p. accepted), labelled axes, scales, accurate plotting, best-fit line (5). (iii) Large triangle, gradient about -0.0104 (range -0.0100 to -0.0110), negative, no unit (3). (iv) ln(V/A) = -Bw with V/A = 0.75 gives w about 27.7 mm; divide by 1.22 mm and round up to 23 slides (4).

items.name: Mean period and uncertainty from timed oscillations
items.how: (i) Explain why timing multiple oscillations improves the measurement of T for a mass on a spring; the extracted stem shows only (i), but the mark scheme also covers (ii) a timing technique (2), (iii) mean T from four 10T readings (2) and (iv) percentage uncertainty in T (2).
items.ms: (i) Measured time is larger (1), absolute uncertainty is constant (1), so percentage uncertainty is reduced (1). (ii) Timing marker at the centre of the oscillation; start timing after several oscillations or use a small displacement (1 each). (iii) Mean 10T = 6.90 s so T = 0.69 s, 2 d.p. (2). (iv) Half range 0.06 s, percentage uncertainty about 0.9% (2); full range scores 0.

items.name: Spring Poisson ratio: technique, uncertainty, material
items.how: (i) Explain one vernier calipers technique for an accurate internal diameter d of a spring; the extracted stem shows only (i), but the mark scheme also covers (ii) percentage uncertainty in D^2/2d^2 (D = 59.4 +/- 0.2 mm, d = 13.9 +/- 0.1 mm) (3) and (iii) whether the spring could be steel with Poisson ratio 0.265 (2).
items.ms: (i) EITHER repeat at different orientations and calculate a mean (1) to reduce random error (1); OR check and correct zero error (1) to eliminate/reduce systematic error (1). (ii) 2 x %U in D + 2 x %U in d = 0.68 + 1.44 = 2.1% (3), or max/min half-range. (iii) Lower limit 0.259 below 0.265, or %D 4.2% < 6%, so could be steel (2).

items.name: Measuring cylinder resolution and percentage uncertainty
items.how: (i) State the resolution of a 500 cm^3 measuring cylinder; (ii) determine the percentage uncertainty in the measured volume of water read from the diagram (the stem text shows 450 cm^3 but the mark scheme uses 480 cm^3).
items.ms: (i) 5 cm^3 (1). (ii) Uses half resolution, 2.5 cm^3 (1); percentage uncertainty 2.5/480 x 100 = 0.5% (0.52% accepted) (1); e.c.f. for the resolution stated in (i).

items.name: Show frequency about 200 Hz from oscilloscope
items.how: Show that the frequency of the microphone signal is about 200 Hz from an oscilloscope trace with a 2.0 ms per division time base.
items.ms: Count the horizontal divisions for at least 2 waves (1); multiply by 2.0 ms and divide by the number of waves to get T = 4.4 ms (1); use f = 1/T (1); f = 227 Hz, stated as about 230 Hz (1).

items.name: Why graph of f against V^-0.5 may be inaccurate
items.how: Explain why results for f against V (three pairs, V = 425, 375, 330 cm^3) plotted as f against V^-0.5 may not give an accurate value of k in f = kV^-0.5.
items.ms: Any four: too few data points; range of data too small; possible systematic error in V; so an accurate best-fit line cannot be drawn; therefore the gradient may not be close to the true value (1 each).

items.name: Safety precautions with a beta source
items.how: Describe two safety precautions when using a beta source.
items.ms: Any two: handle with tongs; use for as short a time as possible; stand away or do not point at the body; store in a lead-lined container (1 each).

items.name: Plan to test count rate varies as 1/d^2
items.how: Devise a plan, including a suitable graph, to test the prediction C = a/d^2 for count rate against distance from a beta source to a G-M tube.
items.ms: Record background count rate and subtract it (1); measure d with a metre rule (1); align source and tube, or keep the rule close, or use a set square (1); count over a long period (at least 1 minute) or repeat and average, or continue until background (1); at least 5 values of d (1); plot C against 1/d^2 and check for a straight line through the origin, or log C against log d with gradient -2 (1).

items.name: Advantage of overfilling above the 50 cm^3 mark
items.how: State one advantage of filling the glass tube with more than 50 cm^3 of glycerol before starting the stopwatch at the 50 cm^3 mark.
items.ms: EITHER removes the delay between opening the tap and starting the stopwatch (or the difficulty of doing both at once), OR allows the flow rate to be constant when timing starts (1). Reaction time references ignored.

items.name: ln V against t graph for glycerol flow
items.how: (i) Explain how a graph of ln V against t gives b for V = 50e^(-bt); the extracted stem shows only (i), but the mark scheme also covers (ii) plotting ln V against t (5), (iii) finding b (3) and (iv) how a higher glycerol temperature would affect the graph (3).
items.ms: (i) ln V = ln 50 - bt compared with y = c + mx, gradient -b (2). (ii) ln V to 3 d.p. (2 d.p. accepted), labelled axes ln(V/cm^3) and t/s, scales, plotting within 1 mm, best-fit line (5). (iii) Large triangle, b between 0.018 and 0.019, 2 or 3 s.f., positive, unit s^-1 (3). (iv) Hotter glycerol is less viscous, flow rate increases, so the graph is steeper (3).

items.name: Zero-error check for micrometer accuracy
items.how: Explain one other technique (besides not overtightening and taking a mean at several places) to improve accuracy of micrometer readings of a metre rule thickness.
items.ms: Check and correct for zero error (1) to eliminate/reduce systematic error (1); MP2 dependent on MP1; 'system/systemic' not accepted.

items.name: Measuring deflection y and its uncertainty
items.how: (i) Describe a method to determine an accurate deflection y of a loaded cantilevered metre rule using another metre rule; the extracted stem shows only (i), but the mark scheme also covers (ii) explaining why the uncertainty in y is 1 mm (3).
items.ms: (i) Clamp the second rule vertical and check with a set square, plumb line or spirit level (1); align zero with the undeflected rule and read the deflected position, or subtract the readings (1); use a set square or place the rules close, or add a pointer, to reduce parallax (1). (ii) Resolution 1 mm (1); uncertainty per reading is half resolution, 0.5 mm (1); two readings so uncertainties add to 1 mm (1).

items.name: Young modulus of rule, uncertainty, material check
items.how: (i) Show that E = 4MgL^3/(w t^3 y) is about 1.6 x 10^10 Pa (M = 0.3982 kg, four w readings, L = 0.798 m, t = 6.17 mm, y = 85 mm); the extracted stem shows only (i), but the mark scheme also covers (ii) percentage uncertainty in E (4) and (iii) whether the rule could be oak of E = 1.23 x 10^10 Pa (2).
items.ms: (i) Mean w = 25.02 mm (1); substitute into E = 4MgL^3/(w t^3 y) (1); E = 1.59 x 10^10 Pa (1). (ii) Half range for w, then %U in L, w, t, y with 3 x %U in L and 3 x %U in t added: 2.7% (4), or max/min half-range method. (iii) Lower limit 1.55 x 10^10 exceeds 1.23 x 10^10, or %D 29% > 2.7%, so not oak (2).

items.name: Timing oscillations: technique and video camera
items.how: Two-part: (i) describe two timing techniques for a trolley oscillating between two springs; (ii) explain how using a video camera could improve the results.
items.ms: (i) Timing marker at the centre of the oscillation (1); start timing after several oscillations or use a small initial displacement (1). (ii) Video can record in slow motion (1), so judging when a whole oscillation is complete is more accurate (1, dependent on MP1).

items.name: Mean period and percentage uncertainty from 5T
items.how: Calculate the mean period T from four 5T readings (5.25, 5.16, 5.21, 5.19 s), then determine the percentage uncertainty in the mean T.
items.ms: (i) Mean 5T = 5.203 s (1) and T = 1.04 s to 2 d.p. (1). (ii) Half range (or furthest value from the mean) = 0.045 s (1); percentage uncertainty about 0.9%, e.c.f., 1 or 2 s.f. (1).

items.name: Criticise recording of mass and period data
items.how: Criticise: a table of trolley mass (1.3, 1.8, 2.3, no units) and T (1.01, 5.90, 1.34) recorded for drawing a graph.
items.ms: Any two from: no units for mass; too few points for a best-fit line; inconsistent T at mass 1.8 (5.90 s); mass should be recorded to more decimal places; no evidence of repeats (1 each).

items.name: Maximum induced e.m.f. from oscilloscope trace
items.how: Determine the maximum e.m.f. induced across a small coil from an oscilloscope trace with the vertical scale at 5 mV per division.
items.ms: Find the number of divisions for the (half) amplitude, 3.7 (1); multiply by 5 mV per division (1); e.m.f. = 18.5 mV, 19 mV accepted (1).

items.name: Circuit and method to find constant z
items.how: (i) Complete the circuit diagram for the large coil on an a.c. supply; (ii) devise a method, using a suitable graph, to determine z in V = zNI/x.
items.ms: (i) Ammeter in series with the large coil (1); variable resistor or potentiometer to vary the current (1). (ii) Measure x with a rule; count N; keep x and N constant; record I and V; at least 5 different sets of values (repeats-and-mean not credited); plot V against I with gradient zN/x (1 each, 6 marks).

items.name: Safety precautions with electrolytic capacitor
items.how: Describe two safety precautions when using a 680 uF electrolytic capacitor in a circuit.
items.ms: Any two: do not exceed the working p.d.; connect with correct polarity; discharge the capacitor fully before handling (1 each).

items.name: ln I against t graph to find resistance
items.how: (i) Explain how a graph of ln I against t gives R for I = I0 e^(-t/RC); the mark scheme also covers (ii) plotting ln I against t from I-t data in mA with a processed-data table (5) and (iii) determining R from the gradient (4), although the extracted stem shows only (i).
items.ms: (i) ln I = ln I0 - t/RC compared with y = c + mx, gradient -1/RC (2). (ii) ln I values to 3 d.p. (2 d.p. accepted), axes ln(I/mA) and t/s, suitable scales, accurate plotting, best-fit line (1 each). (iii) Large triangle (1), gradient = -1/RC (1), R in 3.25 x 10^4 to 3.42 x 10^4 ohm (1), 2 or 3 s.f. with unit (1); example R about 33.8 kohm.

items.name: Data logger versus ammeter and stopwatch
items.how: Explain how a data logger instead of an ammeter and stopwatch would improve the capacitor discharge investigation.
items.ms: EITHER simultaneous readings (1) so values closer to the true value or less uncertainty (1); OR high sampling rate (1) so less uncertainty in the best-fit line (1); MP2 dependent on MP1.

items.name: Accurate method for resonant length L
items.how: Describe an accurate method to find the bridge distance L giving maximum amplitude of a vibrating wire on an a.c. supply.
items.ms: Move the bridge slowly/incrementally to find maximum amplitude, or use card behind the wire (1); use a metre rule to measure L (1); zero of rule at the edge of the blocks, or subtract two readings (1); repeat finding the maximum several times and calculate a mean L (1).

items.name: Micrometer technique for wire diameter
items.how: Explain one technique to determine an accurate value of the wire diameter d with a micrometer screw gauge.
items.ms: EITHER repeat at different positions/orientations and calculate a mean (1) to reduce random errors (1); OR check and correct for zero error (1) to eliminate/reduce systematic error (1); MP2 dependent on MP1; 1 mark for avoiding overtightening if nothing else scores.

items.name: Wire density, uncertainty and material check
items.how: (i) Show that density rho from L^2 = Mg/(pi rho d^2 f^2) is about 8100 kg m^-3 (M = 802 g, d = 1.02 mm, f = 50.3 Hz, L = 0.343 m); the mark scheme also has (ii) show the percentage uncertainty in rho is about 6% (4) and (iii) deduce whether the wire could be stainless steel of density 7800 kg m^-3 (2), although the extracted stem shows only (i).
items.ms: (i) Rearrange to rho = Mg/(pi d^2 f^2 L^2) (1); rho = 8090 kg m^-3 to at least 3 s.f. (1). (ii) %U in d, f (half resolution) and L; 2 x each added; about 5.9% (4), or max/min rho half-range method. (iii) Lower limit 8090 x (1 - 0.059) = 7612 is below 7800 so could be stainless steel (or %D = 3.7% < 5.9%) (1 + 1).
